summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, and the code on single-sex services issued in 2025, bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007 under Gibraltar's own equality provisions.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013, and in July 2026 passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after a bill passed unanimously, a Supreme Court ruling of 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and an Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024 that expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility has surfaced in recent years even where the statute is protective. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation tackling what Chief Minister Fabian Picardo called 'disgusting lurking homophobia' on social media during Pride month, and began examining a proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, prompted by an incident of anti-gay abuse.

Public opinion on relationship recognition has not been uniform. A December 2015 consultation on same-sex marriage left Gibraltarians polarised, with an inter-ministerial committee weighing all viewpoints before the draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act went to Parliament in August 2016; popular consultation and the main parties indicated support for the change.

Family-building routes have widened in ways a trans visitor's family may care about. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination, and in June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.

The direction of travel over two decades has been toward equalisation. Before 2012 gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of consent of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009; the 2011 ruling and the Crimes Act 2011 reversed that position.
localsOnly:
Residents invoke the same equality provisions adopted in 2007, which cover gender reassignment and sexual orientation, and the hate crime and hate speech offences as amended in July 2026 to include transgender identity.

Residents have access to civil partnership, same-sex marriage, adoption under the Adoption Act 2023, altruistic surrogacy under the 2021 law, and assisted reproduction under the health authority's amended in vitro fertilisation policy. Surrogacy eligibility is limited to married couples or civil partners unable to conceive.

The July 2026 conversion therapy offence binds practitioners and those offering such services locally.

Residents are equally without a domestic route to change a legal gender marker; the sourced material records no application procedure, no statutory process and no case law establishing one.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been extended to Gibraltar by Order in Council is unresolved in the sourced material; the sources record no extension, but they are not a register of Orders in Council.

The enforcement record of the gender-reassignment discrimination protection is not sourced. No material addresses complaints, tribunal or court outcomes, or penalties applied under that provision.

No sourced material covers border screening practice, document inspection of gender markers by Gibraltar or United Kingdom officers, visa conditions for trans travellers, prison placement, or access to transition-related healthcare for visitors.

Royal assent and commencement dates for the two bills passed in July 2026, covering transgender identity in hate crime and hate speech legislation and the conversion therapy offence, are not stated in the sources; only passage by Parliament is recorded.

Several legal-history claims rest on a single open-source chain: one of the cited pages is a mirror of the same Wikipedia article used elsewhere, so corroboration is weaker than the number of links suggests.

The Foreign Affairs Committee report's material on corruption concerns Turks and Caicos and has no bearing on Gibraltar; only its governance expectations and its 2008 recommendation on sexual orientation and gender status are used here.
